16385236 function|malloc|free
16385260 FuncAddress
16385344 This command allows you to call an arbitrary function in the code.  It also provides specific support for common functions (such as malloc/free).  When calling a function, you specify the address of the function (which must come from the MAP file for your image).  You can also specify up to 9 parameters to the function.  Additionally, you can specify whether or not the function returns anything, allowing the return value to be printed.
16385785 NOTE:  While this command is very useful for tricky debug situations in the field, IT IS SERIOUSLY UNSAFE!  You can easily crash the system you are trying to debug if you specify a function address or parameter incorrectly.  You could even brick the system if the function happens to write to permanent nonvol at the wrong time, or corrupts the bootloader, or...you get the picture.  Make sure you are working with a valid MAP file for the image that is running, as this is your only hope for getting things right!  Also, make sure you provide exactly the number of function parameters that are needed for the function.  Entering too few or too many parameters will cause registers and stack state to be wrong for the function, and will lead to mayhem.
16386539 Functions that require more than 9 parameters cannot be called, and they are unlikely candidates for this type of thing anyway.  We chose to allow 9 because C++ methods use the first parameter as the object pointer (e.g. the 'this' pointer), which allows up to 8 real parameters to the method.
16386834 The first command parameter must be one of the following:
16386892   'function' - causes the function address (specified by -a) to be called with however many function parameters are specified.
16387019   'malloc' - causes malloc() to be called with the value specified by the first function parameter.
16387119   'free' - causes free() to be called with the value specified by the first function parameter.
16387216 The remaining command parameters are:
16387254   -r indicates that the function returns a value, and that the return value should be printed.  If left out, the return value (if any) is not printed.  The value is not interpreted, it is simply printed as a uint32 value in decimal and hex.
16387495   -a specifies the address of the function to be called.  This is only used for 'call function', since the other named functions know which address they are calling.
16387661   Param1..9 specify up to 9 parameters to be passed to the function.  Make sure you specify the correct number of function parameters (and that they are in the right order).  Note that when calling C++ methods, the first parameter is used to hold the object instance (e.g. the 'this' pointer).  For functions that take no parameters, don't specify any parameters here.
16388031 One of the interesting aspects of this command is that it allows you to allocate memory, write to it, call a function with it, then free it.  
16388176 Calls malloc(1024); the allocated memory address is printed:
16388237   call malloc -r 1024
16388259 Calls free(0x80001234) to free memory that had previously been allocated:
16388333   call free 0x80001234
16388356 Calls the function at address 0x80010080 with no parameters.  Return value not printed:
16388444   call func -a 0x80010080
16388470 Calls the function at address 0x800100a0 with a single parameter (value 0x01) and prints the return value:
16388577   call func -r -a 0x800100a0 0x01

16662409 The value may be specified in any of the following three ways:
16662473 1: If the value is between 0.25 and 10 then it is treated as a relative value above 51 expressed in units of dB.
16662586 2: If the value is between 51.25 and 61 then it is treated as an absolute value expressed in units of dB.
16662692 3: If the value is between 205 and 244 then it is treated as an absolute value expressed in units of dB/4 (TLV format).

16662877 1: The same modulation format must be used for all upstream channels.
16662947 2: Distortion will increased. It will comply with DOCSIS requirements, but will no longer comply with the extended Comcast specifications for downstream spurious signals from 54 to 88 MHz.
16663136 3: Extended power will be increased approximately 3 dB for 64-QAM and 16-QAM formats ONLY, This level of power enhancement will only be achievable on North American low-split systems (42 MHz upper limit).

16890244 General command format:  cmd [(#)] [parms...]
16890291 'cmd' is the command to be executed.  Type 'help' to get a list of available
16890368 commands.  Note that the parser can handle partial command names (e.g. 'he'
16890444 for 'help').  It always selects the first good match that it finds.
16890513 '(#)' is the optional set or range of instance numbers.  If specified, then
16890589 the command is only executed for those instances.  If absent, then the command
16890668 is executed for all registered instances.  The instance numbers are delimited
16890746 by one of a space, comma, or semicolon (e.g. '(0, 1; 2 3)').  A range is
16890819 delimited by a dash (e.g. '(0-3)').  You can specify an open-ended range that
16890897 goes to the end of the instances (e.g. '(3-)'), and you can specify mixes of
16890974 values (e.g. '(0 - 3, 5, 7-)').
16891007 'parms' are the optional parameters for the command.  See the help information
16891086 for the command for details on the parameters.
16891134 Note that all strings and parameters are case-sensitive, so 'help' is not the
16891212 same as 'Help', and '-i' is not the same as '-I'.
16891263 While entering a command, typing a '?' will display the help for that command,
16891342 then will restore the line you were entering so you can finish the command.
16891419 Each command can have 0 or more parameters, and there are different types of
16891496 parameters (each with their own parsing syntax):
16891545   Boolean - Accepts 1/t/T/y/Y as 'true'; 0/f/F/n/N as 'false'.
16891608   Flag - A '-' followed by a single character; may also be followed by one
16891683     command parameter (e.g. '-s', '-i IpAddress', '-n Unsigned Int').
16891753   Float - An IEEE single-precision (32-bit) floating point number (0, 7.5, 0.3,
16891833     1.3e-5).  The valid range for the value will be shown after the name as
16891909     {min..max} if it is limited.
16891942   IpAddress - A dotted decimal IP address, such as '192.168.100.1'.
16892010   MacAddress - A colon-delimited hex MAC address, such as '00:10:18:de:ad:01'.
16892089   SignedInt - A signed integer value (32-bit), in hex or decimal.  The valid
16892166     range for the value will be shown after the name as {min..max}.
16892234   UnsignedInt - An unsigned integer value (32-bit), in hex or decimal.  The
16892310     valid range for the value will be shown after the name as {min..max}.
16892384   String - A string value, delimited by whitespace.  If you need to enter a
16892460     string with spaces, enclose it with quotes (e.g. "String with spaces").
16892536     If you need to enter an empty string, use "" or the word NULL as the
16892609     value.  The max length of the string is shown after the name as {length}.
16892687   StringSet - An enum-like entry method.  Accepts one of the string values
16892762     listed, which is translated to a number 0..n-1, where n is the number of
16892839     strings.
16892852   Bitmask - Allows you to enter a bitmask value in decimal or hex.  A bitmask
16892930     may only allow some bits to be specified; these are shown in help text as
16893008     {0xNN} after the parameter name.  If nothing is shown, all 32 bits are
16893083     valid.  Additionally, you can specify one of these special characters
16893157     before the value to modify the existing value:
16893208       '=' - store the value ('=0x20' -> value  = 0x20)
16893263       '&' - bitwise AND     ('&0x20' -> value &= 0x20)
16893318       '|' - bitwise OR      ('|0x20' -> value |= 0x20)
16893373       '~' - invert/AND      ('~0x20' -> value &= ~0x20)

16898344 The V2 console works very much like a DOS or Unix command line interface.  It
16898422 allows you to enter commands to the system, controlling various objects.  The
16898500 console supports the following features:
16898542 Subdirectories - The commands are grouped into DOS-like subdirectories, where
16898620     each subdir is associated with a subsystem in the application.  Use the
16898696     'cd' command to change the current dir.  There are a group of commands that
16898776     are always available regardless of what subdir you are in.  Use the 'help'
16898855     command to see the commands that are available for the subdir.
16898923 Multiple instance support - Each command is executed for an instance of an
16898998     object in the system.  Often, there is only one instance, but in some cases
16899078     there can be multiple instances.  When executing a command, you can select
16899157     all, one, or a set of instances using special command format.  Type
16899229     'help -u' for the command format to select instances.
16899288 Command name expansion - When you type part of a command name and hit space,
16899365     tab, or enter, the parser will automatically expand the partial name out to
16899445     its full name.  This helps clarify exactly which command will be executed,
16899524     especially when there are multiple commands that match the partial string.
16899603     If there are no commands that match the partial string, then the console
16899680     will beep at you, giving feedback that the command is not valid.
16899750 Special key handling - The V2 console supports the following special keys:
16899825     Left/Right Arrow, Home/End, Ctl-Left, Ctl-Right Arrow:  These move the
16899900         cursor, changing the point at which new characters will be inserted.
16899977         The console does not support overwriting, only insertion.
16900043     Up/Down Arrow:  These scroll back/forward through the command history,
16900118         showing commands that had previously been executed.
16900178     Del:  Deletes the character at the cursor.
16900225     Backspace:  Deletes the character before the cursor, moving the cursor back
16900305         one space.
16900324     Esc:  Aborts the command that is currently being entered.
16900386     ?:  When entering a command, pressing '?' will show you the help for that
16900464         command, including parameters.
16900504 For ANSI or VT100 type terminal emulators (CRT, HyperTerm, etc.), you may need
16900583 to configure the keyboard mapping in order for some of the special keys to be
16900661 handled properly:
16900679   Esc:  0x1b                      Del:  0x7f                Backspace:  0x08
16900756   Up Arrow:        0x1b 5b 41 'Esc[A'    Down Arrow:      0x1b 5b 42 'Esc[B'
16900833   Right Arrow:     0x1b 5b 43 'Esc[C'    Left Arrow:      0x1b 5b 44 'Esc[D'

17251292 eth_autoneg
17251304 Enables or disables the ethernet autonegotiation feature.  If enabled, the ethernet driver will automatically detect and negotiate the link speed and duplex parameters, allowing it to coexist on various networks.  If disabled, then the ethernet driver will use the link parameters stored in NonVol Settings, which may cause collisions and/or link errors if they are not set correctly.  In general, you will want to leave autonegotiation on, but there are some cases where it is desirable or necessary to set the link manually. You must reboot for this to take effect!

17610336 start_size

17610640 end_size
17610652 Sets or shows the size of the largest ping packet that will be sent (including LLC and IP header overhead).  After the packet size is increased by the step amount, if it is larger than this value, then the size is reset to the start size.  This must be between start_size..1518 (MTU), inclusive.
17610948 end_size 1518	Sets the end size to the maximum allowed.
17611004 step_amount
17611016 Sets or shows the amount that the packet size will be increased for each packet.  This can be any number (including 0, which means to keep the size constant for every packet).  Note that if you set it too large, then the packet size will wrap around to the start size every time, since it will never be allowed to be larger than the end_size.  You can also specify a negative number which causes the ping size to start with the end size parameter and step down to the start size, then wrap back around to the end size.
17611536 step_amount 1	Increases the packet size by 1 each time.
17611592 step_amount -1	Decreases the packet size by 1 each time.
17611652 time_between_pings
17611672 Milliseconds
17611688 Sets or shows the number of milliseconds that the ping helper will wait before sending the next ping.  Note that this does not include time spent waiting for the reply or verifying it, or for time spent printing status information.  The actual resolution and accuracy of this depends on the system (pSOS generally runs with a 10ms clock tick, so 10ms is the same as 15ms on that system).
17612076 time_between_pings 100	Waits 100ms before sending the next ping.
17612144 wait_enable
17612156 Enables/disables waiting for ping replies.  If enabled, the ping helper will wait a number of milliseconds for the reply, and will process it if received.  This is true even if the timeout is 0ms; it will always check for and process the response.  If disabled, then no attempt will be made to check for or process a response.  This is generally only of interest when you need to send data very quickly, with no variability.
17612584 wait_enable 1	Enables waiting for the ping reply.
17612636 wait_time
17612648 Sets or shows the number of milliseconds that the ping helper will wait for a ping response before continuing.  This only takes effect if waiting is enabled.  The actual resolution and accuracy of this depends on the system (pSOS generally runs with a 10ms clock tick, so 10ms is the same as 15ms on that system).
17612964 wait_time 5000	Sets the reply wait timeout to 5 seconds.
17613024 verify_enable

17613316 verbosity
17613328 Sets the level of information that will be displayed while pinging.  A higher number provides more information, but also slows down the rate at which pings can be sent.  Most host-based ping utilities provide output equivalent to 3.  For high-performance, high packet rate pings, values of 1 or 2 are best.

17744056 This enables/disables logging for packets received from the specified interfaces and being sent to the specified interfaces.  If enabled, then the contents of the packet will be displayed, and the forwarder will show info about the HalIf on which it was received/sent, as well as why the packet was dropped.  If the from/to interfaces parameters are missing, then all will be done.  The interfaces are a bitmask where 0x01 corresponds to the interface at index 0, 0x04 corresponds to the interface at index 2, etc.

19901055 	-m  sets HT rates (bitmasks, 00-ff). Least significant bit is MCS0.
19901124 	    example: 'rateset -m 0x3f 0x01' limits rates to MCS0-MCS5 and MCS8
19901197 	-v  sets VHT MCS values for each supported count of spatial streams.
19901267 	    example: 'rateset -v 3ff 1ff ff' limits vht rates to MCS 0-9 for 1 stream,
19901347 	                             MCS 0-8 for 2 streams, and MCS 0-7 for 3 streams.
19901428 txbf_rateset
19901444 Get rateset consisting of OFDM, HT and VHT rates, and Broadcom-to-Broadcom
19901519 	group of OFDM, HT and VHT rates by issuing command with no arguments.
19901590 	OFDM rates printed are in Mbps, and each Basic rate in OFDM list is marked
19901666 	by (b) behind it.  Example: full list of OFDM rates:
19901720 		6(b) 9 12(b) 18 24(b) 36 48 54
19901753 	where 6, 12 and 24 are Basic rates.
19901791 	Set synopsis:
19901806 		wl txbf_rateset < [ofdm_rate_list] [options ...] >
19901859 	OFDM rate specification does not need to mark Basic rates because Basic
19901932 	rates are automatically recognized.
19901969 	Options are processed in order; thus redundant instances of an option will
19902045 	result in only the last instance taking effect for that option.
19902110 	Options:
19902120 	-m <MCS_bitmask> ...
19902142 		Set HT rates by bitmask bytes, each ranges from 00 through ff, where
19902213 		the least significant bit is MCS0.
19902250 		Example: '-m 3f 01' specifies HT rates MCS0 - MCS5 and MCS8.
19902314 	-v <VHT_bitmask> ...
19902336 		Set VHT rates for each supported count of spatial streams.
19902397 		Example: '-v 3ff 1ff ff' specifies VHT rates: MCS0 - MCS9 for 1 stream,
19902471 		MCS0 - MCS8 for 2 streams, and MCS0 - MCS7 for 3 streams.
19902536 		Set for Broadcom-to-Broadcom group of rates.  Otherwise without
19902602 		the -b option, the standard group of rates are set accordingly.
